newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bomb kills 12 in Algeria, troops battle Moslem rebels.
newsitem.headline: Bomb kills 12 in Algeria, troops battle Moslem rebels.

text.p: A powerful bomb ripped through a crowded car market near Algiers on Thursday, killing at least 12 people and wounding about 100, some seriously, according to hospital sources.
Medical sources said more than 100 wounded people had been taken to several hospitals, including in Boufarik, Blida and Algiers.
The bomb went off just hours after gunfire blasted the heart of Algiers in what residents said was a battle between security forces and Moslem rebels trapped there.
"According to a provisional toll (the bomb) killed 12 people and wounded several, some of whom are in a serious condition," Algerian security forces said.
Car markets, mainly selling second-hand cars, attract thousands of people, often in family groups with children, during the Algerian weekend of Thursday and Friday.
Boufarik, known as a haunt of Moslem fundamentalists trying to overthrow the government of President Liamine Zeroual, lies some 30 km (20 miles) south of Algiers.

The bomb exploded at 10 a.m. (0900 GMT), in apparent challenge to Zeroual's statement on Wednesday to the cabinet, his first this year, that "terrorism will be fought with determination and the state will keep its pledges..."

Zeroual's remarks were his first on "terrorism" this year which has been marked by more rebel attacks against villages, and by bombings, mostly in Algiers and surrounding towns. More than 300 people have been killed since early November.

Early this week, the bodies of five girls, their throats cut, were found in Chebli village near Algiers. The discovery was made the same day villagers were burying 14 people in neighbouring Tabainat village. All died the same violent way.

Thursday's security force statement on Algeria's official news agency APS did not indicate who the authorities believed responsible for the Boufarik bomb, the third in eight days. But they have blamed previous such attacks on the Moslem rebels.
The security forces, according to diplomats and subsequent newspaper reports unchallenged by the authorities, frequently understate the numbers killed or wounded.

Two bomb attacks eight days ago killed 20 people and wounded more than 100 in Algiers and Ain-Fakroun town, 380 km (240 miles), east of the city. At least 1,400 people have died in bomb attacks in the past five years.

On the authorities' side, Algerian security forces swept on Wednesday night into the heights of the Casbah, the ancient heart of the old city overlooking the Mediterranean, to try to eliminate about 12 guerrillas holed up there.
Residents said the forces, deployed near the gendarmerie headquarters, were backed by crack troops sent in three hours after the battle started at about 7 p.m. (1800 GMT).
"We then heard explosions, apparently grenades thrown by security forces into the gunmen's hideout," said one resident.
Sporadic gunfire and explosions could be heard until 2 a.m. (0100 GMT) on Thursday, the residents said.
Algerian authorities have made no statement on the clash.

Security forces have several times ringed and combed the Casbah and killed dozens of guerrillas in its winding streets in the past three years. Very few prisoners have been taken, and security forces have used heavy weaponry to blast houses sheltering guerrillas.

The Casbah was a centre of Algerian resistance against French forces in Algeria's 1954-1962 war of independence, and French troops fought for months to try to end resistance and destroy bomb-making "factories" there, never fully succeeding.
Residents said the guerrillas had built up their forces in the Casbah and made their presence known with the cold-blooded killing of more than 20 people there in the past four months.
The Armed Islamic Group recently posted leaflets on Casbah walls warning they would kill women who still wore Western dress and banning men from smoking and reading newspapers.
About 60,000 people have been killed in Algeria's violence since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a commanding lead.
